item.title: 🔴 New GeoServer RCE exploit chain seen in the wild two days after disclosure
item.description:
Why this matters: Remote-code-execution risk — assess exposure and patch or mitigate quickly.

Attackers have begun probing a chain of five GeoServer vulnerabilities that enables unauthenticated remote code execution, just two days after the open source geospatial server project disclosed the flaws.

Security firm watchTowr, which operates a global network of honeypot servers, reported that it observed the probing activity in the early morning hours of Wednesday. Attackers from multiple IP addresses created stored queries on GeoServer instances, checked whether they were created, and deleted them immediately, a technique that confirms a server is vulnerable without delivering a malicious payload.

GeoServer is widely used by government agencies, utilities, and large organizations to publish maps and geospatial data, and it has become a recurring target for attackers. The full RCE chain was reported to the project in August by Jonah Burgess, a senior security researcher at Rapid7 who uses the online handle CryptoCat. The GeoServer project shipped fixes in October and early…

item.title: 🟠 Palo Alto confirms Fragnesia exploitation against firewalls in PHP2Shell attacks
item.description:
Why this matters: Credential/phishing risk — reinforce MFA and watch for suspicious sign-ins.

Palo Alto Networks has confirmed that attackers exploited Fragnesia, a Linux kernel flaw, to gain root on PAN-OS firewalls through the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities, and has shipped fixes six months after the bug was patched in Linux.

The vulnerability allows a locally authenticated, low-privileged attacker to escalate privileges to root.

“Exploitation of CVE-2026-46300 has been observed targeting the Palo Alto Networks management interface exposed to the internet,” the company said in its November 25 security advisory. It added that all observed attacks targeted devices whose management interface “is exposed to the internet, a configuration our best practices advise against.”

Even so, the company labeled the bulletin “Informational” and gave it no CVSS score. Fixed builds span every supported PAN-OS branch from 10.2 to 12.2.

A second patch cycle in a month

item.title: 🟠 Prompting AI to be ‘thorough’ can drive sandbox escapes, Anthropic says
item.description:
Why this matters: Credential/phishing risk — reinforce MFA and watch for suspicious sign-ins.

Prompt wording meant to make AI agents more resourceful, such as telling them to search thoroughly or invoking authority, sharply raises the odds they will reach outside a poorly secured sandbox, Anthropic has found in its latest evaluation.

The evaluation, called Siren, gives Claude models routine dev-ops tasks inside deliberately weakened sandboxes and places a “honeypot,” such as a credential, file, or emulated internet service, outside the boundary, Anthropic researchers Oscar O’Rahilly and Darya Kaviani wrote in a blog post.

Anthropic tested six Claude models, from Mythos 5 to the 5.5 series, without the safeguards that ship in its products. The tests covered more than 1,700 scenarios in 26 sandboxes built on tools including Docker, gVisor, and QEMU. Most of the weaknesses are misconfigurations modeled on public reports, the company said.

Wording mattered more than deadlines

item.title: 🟠 Despite doom and gloom headlines, AI attacks are thin on the ground
item.description:
Why this matters: Credential/phishing risk — reinforce MFA and watch for suspicious sign-ins.

When Anthropic announced its Mythos AI model, it was touted as being so cyber capable that only a handful of organizations could have early access to harden their defenses before the public — and attackers — got their hands on the technology.

Soon after, AI companies, one after the other, warned that their AI models were smart enough to discover previously unknown exploits and escape containment.

And a new worldview took hold, that security organizations were soon to see a wave of new kinds of attacks, never seen before, and every company was at risk — unless it immediately started using the latest and greatest AI to defend against all these new threats.

Has that happened? Well, kind of.

What CISOs are seeing

In the first quarter of 2026, RSAC asked Fortune 1000 CISOs whether they’d seen definitive evidence of AI-powered attack techniques being used against their companies, beyond social engineering, and 44% said yes.

item.title: 🟠 Cisco and OpenAI dispatch AI agents to shield vulnerable systems before permanent patches arrive
item.description:
Why this matters: Endpoint-security changes may affect detection and alerting.

Autonomous AI agents are rapidly and dramatically transforming the cybersecurity landscape for both defenders and adversaries.

In hopes of giving security teams a head start and pitting machine against machine, Cisco and OpenAI have released a new open source project, dubbed Shirudo (Japanese for “shield”). The Shirudo platform launches small, temporary mitigations to help protect systems until patches can be deployed. AI agents can replace flawed code with fixed code, which human teams can test and approve (or not), then deploy, setting boundaries and holding onto the keys, with no need for a hard reset.

The project has already been proven to block a Java4Shell exploit attempt against the search and analytics platform Elasticsearch, while the site continued to run as usual.

Need to buy time

item.title: 🟠 Attackers exploited an Azure API Management flaw to steal secrets, Microsoft warns
item.description:
Why this matters: Credential/phishing risk — reinforce MFA and watch for suspicious sign-ins.

Microsoft is warning customers that attackers exploited a flaw in Azure API Management Classic tiers to steal stored secrets, an intrusion that Norway’s National Security Authority has linked to breaches at two energy companies and says organizations should assume exposed credentials were compromised.

Microsoft said in an Azure Service Health security advisory sent to customers that it identified the vulnerability on Nov. 18 and deployed a mitigation the following day. The advisory, tracking ID MZK9-GH0, said the exposure began before Microsoft found the flaw, reported Bleeping Computer.

The company said in the advisory that “an unauthorized party could have used the issue to access secrets stored in Azure API Management Classic instances.”

item.title: 🟠 CrowdStrike buys missing network security piece in $43.9B Zscaler deal
item.description:
Why this matters: Service impact is possible — verify vendor status before troubleshooting internally.

CrowdStrike agreed to acquire cloud security company Zscaler in a $43.9 billion all-stock deal on Monday, combining endpoint protection with zero-trust network security in one of the largest cybersecurity acquisitions ever and intensifying the industry’s race to build broad security platforms.

The deal brings together CrowdStrike’s Falcon platform, which focuses on endpoint, identity and cloud security, with Zscaler’s cloud-delivered network security and zero-trust access capabilities. CrowdStrike said the combined company is expected to begin with more than $10 billion in annual recurring revenue (ARR).

The acquisition also addresses a strategic gap in CrowdStrike’s portfolio. While the company has expanded beyond endpoint protection into identity, cloud security and threat intelligence, Zscaler brings an established security service edge (SSE) and zero-trust network access platform.

For all the talk of AI use by attackers and defenders, little attention is paid to ways CISOs and their security pros can leverage AI uniquely to expediate tasks, cut through the noise, facilitate decision-making, and potentially save big on auditing.

Several specific AI prompts can help security leaders and staff handle multiple critical tasks not typically associated with AI for cyber defense, such as risk management, compliance, policy development, and critical thinking.

Developing truly useful prompts isn’t particularly easy, however, because it often requires a significant amount of research and effort, not to mention lots of fine-tuning, which can take security teams away from other critical tasks. Fortunately, the security community is here to help, with advice on unique prompt ideas that have greatly aided them in strengthening security, facilitating decision-making, and saving time for hands-on defense.

item.title: 🔴 PHP2Shell aftershock: 18 more PHP flaws put enterprise web admins on alert
item.description:
Why this matters: Credential/phishing risk — reinforce MFA and watch for suspicious sign-ins.

PHP continues to root out flaws in its architecture, this week releasing fixes for a slew of additional security issues in the wake of PHP2Shell.

The patches address 18 vulnerabilities, including a critical request smuggling flaw that could allow unauthenticated attackers to remotely execute code on vulnerable servers. Other vulnerabilities affect PHP’s core engine, session handling, process manager, and Common Gateway Interface (CGI) protocol, which bridges web servers with external application programs.

The updates were released for all supported PHP versions, with PHP 8.5.13, 8.4.28, 8.3.37, and 8.2.36 containing the fixes.

item.title: 🔵 Do AI’s mathematical advances put PKI under threat?
item.description:
Why this matters: Could affect sign-ins, MFA, or Conditional Access — watch for authentication issues.

Warnings by a leading cryptographer that industry-wide public-key cryptography could fail because of advances in AI has sparked a debate in the security community.

In a series of post on X, Johns Hopkins cryptographer Matthew Green warned that existing public-key cryptography systems were at risk because machines have begun outperforming humans in their ability to address some mathematical problems.

“I think there is a 1% chance we live in Minicrypt, and a 15% chance we functionally lose confidence in our existing public-key encryption algorithms,” Green wrote last month.

Green’s initial warning and follow-up comments offered a warning about the cryptographic foundations beneath public key infrastructure (PKI), rather than an obituary for PKI, the system of certificates, keys, and certificate authorities that secures Transport Layer Security (TLS), code signing, and many other information security functions.

item.title: 🔴 A single pull request could have handed attackers the keys to Microsoft’s software supply chain
item.description:
Why this matters: Supply-chain risk — review third-party access and affected vendor dependencies.

The most dangerous actor in a software supply chain may now be an automated script with powerful credentials and no idea where it’s sending them.

Researchers from pen-testing company Cycode have discovered a now patched critical zero-click supply chain vulnerability in the open-source Windows Package Manager (WinGet), which sits on billions of devices worldwide.

A single pull request could have tricked Microsoft’s internal tooling into freely handing over a moderator’s GitHub access token, with no phishing, no malware, no moderator clicking or approval required.

There is currently no evidence that the flaw has been exploited in the wild. But it serves as a cautionary tale for enterprises that the automation they trust is becoming an attacker entry point, and package repositories are particularly enticing targets.

Barely a week after the US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) warned companies of the cyber attacker interest in an open source penetration testing tool called ARTEX, the European Commission has confirmed that attackers armed with that tool broke into its HR systems.

The attack, which Commission officials detected on October 22, forced them to shut off much of the access to the systems for more than 10 days.

“As a protective and preventive measure, we temporarily took down several applications and most of them have since then been restored,” Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier said Thursday. “We have not detected any evidence of a data breach affecting Commission staff as a whole.”

During a news media briefing, a transcript of which was provided to CSOonline, he said that the European Data Protection Supervisor (EDPS) was informed of the attack, “so there was no hiding whatsoever.”

item.description:
Why this matters: Authentication bypass — review access controls and look for unauthorized access.

The company’s advisory describes the flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-123890, as “an authentication bypass vulnerability in the VMware Directory Service,” that could let a threat actor with network access gain unauthorized access to the system, and says there are no workarounds. item.title: 🔴 Vulnerability management: The cybersecurity industry is still solving the wrong problem
item.description:
Why this matters: Could affect sign-ins, MFA, or Conditional Access — watch for authentication issues.

We have never been short of vulnerabilities. We have always struggled with remedial work.

For decades, the cybersecurity industry has approached vulnerability management from the wrong end. The emphasis has consistently been on finding vulnerabilities, cataloguing them, scoring them and, more recently, prioritising them through increasingly sophisticated risk models.

An entire industry has developed around vulnerability scanning, exposure management, threat intelligence and remediation prioritization. Artificial intelligence is now promising to take those capabilities to another level.

But there is something fundamentally wrong with that approach.

The real challenge in vulnerability management has never been identifying what needs fixing. It has always been getting the remedial work done.

Most large organizations already know they have significant numbers of vulnerabilities across their technology estates. They have known for years. They have dashboards, reports, inventories, r…

item.title: 🔴 AI unearths ‘internet breaker’ flaws in Nginx web server
item.description:
Why this matters: Remote-code-execution risk — assess exposure and patch or mitigate quickly.

Nginx, the web server estimated to power a third of the internet, has shipped fixes for multiple vulnerabilities, including a critical unauthenticated remote code execution flaw that puts millions of websites at risk and has existed in the code for over a decade. Researchers from several security firms independently found some of the same flaws by using AI agents, adding to a string of recent AI-discovered vulnerabilities in widely used internet technologies such as PHP, Node, OpenSSH, and Java.

The most severe flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-123007, lets an attacker manipulate flow-control windows in the HTTP/2 protocol implementation to trigger an out-of-bounds memory copy that researchers from Xint.io turned into command execution with Nginx worker privileges. The vulnerability affects every official Nginx release for more than 10 years since version 1.9.5, which originally added HTTP/2 support in 2015.

Source: CSO Online  |  Severity: Critical  |  Age: 8d

item.title: 🔴 A new critical Java hole illustrates the enterprise IT visibility problem
item.description:
Why this matters: Credential/phishing risk — reinforce MFA and watch for suspicious sign-ins.

When cybersecurity research firm Calif published details Tuesday of a potentially major Java security flaw, dubbed Java4Shell, it described an unauthenticated attacker’s ability to read Java heap memory, steal private keys, tokens, and session secrets, and reach remote code execution (RCE).

With Java being all-but-ubiquitous in today’s enterprise, coupled with the inability of CISOs to have visibility into every instance of it in their estate, this means that the bug could be a big problem for IT.

Java, which has had its fair share of cybersecurity issues lately, is well-known for safely handling memory. That is why a Java bug affecting memory management is so dangerous. item.title: 🟠 Attackers Used Optimizely to A/B Test Malware on Top Websites
item.description:
Why this matters: Service impact is possible — verify vendor status before troubleshooting internally.
At least 178 top web destinations unwittingly served a variety of malware exploits against visitors over the past 24 hours thanks to a security vulnerability involving Optimizely, a company that helps websites customize user experiences and test out new features. Experts say the incident, which saw data-stealing malicious software silently injected into sites like the BBC, CNN, Equifax, Ledger and Zoom, was exacerbated by the reality that few popular websites enforce strict rules on the sources of third-party content.

Source: Krebs on Security  |  Severity: Important  |  Age: 8d

But even top Russian hackers make operational security mistakes, and the administrator of Qilin has made a few key missteps over the last decade that all point to a 36-year-old man living in St. Petersburg, Russia.

This month's Patch Tuesday addresses 63 critical flaws -- including a zero-day in Microsoft Outlook -- and comes amid important security updates from other software makers, including Adobe, Apple, Google and Mozilla.

item.title: 🔵 Want to Rent an Internet Address at the White House?
item.description:
Why this matters: Regulatory/compliance context — assess scope and action timeline.
Several staffers at the White House are using computers or mobile devices equipped with residential proxy services that render their internet address available for others to rent, security experts warned today. One of the proxy services is a Russian company whose founder's web hosting business was ground zero for cyberattacks against election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.

Source: Krebs on Security  |  Severity: FYI  |  Age: 21d

item.title: 🔵 Tech Firms Dismantle Botnet That Turned 1.3M TV Boxes Into Proxies
item.description:
Why this matters: Regulatory/compliance context — assess scope and action timeline.
Google said today it worked with industry partners to dismantle a botnet made up of more than 1.3 million Android TV set-top boxes that ship with malicious software which secretly rents the user's Internet connection out to strangers and conducts advertising fraud. Experts involved in the takedown say the action is likely to sever the botnet's access to more than 10 million additional compromised systems, including other Internet of Things (IoT) products such as Android-based healthcare devices and karaoke machines.

Source: Krebs on Security  |  Severity: FYI  |  Age: 24d
